                                             D.C. Nos.

PATRICK WAYNE ANDERSON,
                                            OPINION
            Defendant - Appellant.

       Appeal from the United States District Court
                 for the District of Idaho
         David C. Nye, District Judge, Presiding

         Argued and Submitted February 5, 2026
                   Portland, Oregon

                 Filed October 19, 2026

Before: Carlos T. Bea, Morgan B. Christen, and Roopali H.
                  Desai, Circuit Judges.

                 Opinion by Judge Desai
 2                        USA V. ANDERSON


                          SUMMARY *


                        28 U.S.C. § 2255

    The panel vacated the district court’s order denying
Patrick Anderson’s pro se motion to vacate, set aside, or
correct his sentence under 28 U.S.C. § 2255, and remanded.
     Anderson—who pleaded guilty to possession with intent
to distribute methamphetamine and fentanyl, and waived his
right to appeal his conviction and sentence—alleged that his
trial counsel was ineffective because he failed to file an
appeal after Anderson directed him to do so.
   The district court directed Anderson’s trial counsel to
address Anderson’s allegations, and counsel filed a
declaration denying the allegations. The district court
denied the § 2255 motion without a hearing.
    The panel held that, faced with conflicting sworn
statements from Anderson and his trial counsel on a
dispositive issue, the district court should have held a
hearing to assess each person’s credibility, and abused its
discretion by failing to do so before denying Anderson’s
motion. Disagreeing with the government’s argument that
this is a rare case in which credibility can be “conclusively
decided” without a hearing, the panel wrote that Anderson’s
allegations are not “so far outside the bounds of reason” that
they are “impossible to believe.” The panel thus vacated the
order denying Anderson’s § 2255 motion and remanded for
an evidentiary hearing.

*
 This summary constitutes no part of the opinion of the court. It has
been prepared by court staff for the convenience of the reader.
                       USA V. ANDERSON                       3


                        COUNSEL

Christopher A. Booker (argued), Assistant United States
Attorney; Justin D. Whatcott, Acting United States
Attorney; Office of the United States Attorney, United States
Department of Justice, Boise, Idaho; for Plaintiff-Appellee.
Craig H. Durham (argued), Ferguson Durham PLLC, Boise,
Idaho, for Defendant-Appellant.



                         OPINION

DESAI, Circuit Judge:

    Patrick Anderson moved to vacate, set aside, or correct
his sentence under 28 U.S.C. § 2255. He alleged that his trial
counsel was ineffective because he failed to appeal after
Anderson directed him to do so. The district court directed
Anderson’s trial counsel to address Anderson’s allegations,
and counsel filed a declaration denying the allegations.
Faced with conflicting sworn statements from Anderson and
his trial counsel on a dispositive issue, the district court
should have held a hearing to assess each person’s
credibility, and it abused its discretion by failing to do so
before denying Anderson’s motion. We thus vacate the order
denying Anderson’s § 2255 motion and remand for an
evidentiary hearing.
                        Background
    Anderson was indicted for possession with intent to
distribute methamphetamine and fentanyl, unlawful
possession of a firearm, and possession of a firearm in
 4                      USA V. ANDERSON


furtherance of a drug trafficking crime. After the district
court denied Anderson’s motion to suppress evidence, he
pled guilty to possession with intent to distribute. In his plea
agreement, Anderson waived his right to appeal his
conviction and sentence. Both Anderson and his trial counsel
signed the plea agreement and affirmed that Anderson had
been advised of its contents.
    Six months after he was sentenced, Anderson filed a
verified pro se motion to vacate, set aside, or correct his
sentence under 28 U.S.C. § 2255. He also requested an
evidentiary hearing. The motion alleged, in relevant part:

       Movant did not receive effective assistance
       of counsel as guaranteed by the Sixth
       Amendment to the United States Constitution
       for trial counsel[’]s failure to file an appeal.
       After the court[’]s imposition of sentence,
       and after movant had directed trial counsel to
       file an appeal.
       [] After the sentencing hearing Anderson
       discussed with trial counsel his desire to
       appeal. As of this day no appeal has been
       filed. After suppression motion was denied,
       movant requested trial counsel to appeal
       decision. As of this day no appeal has been
       filed.
       According to Roe v. Flores-Ortega, 528 U.S.
       470, 145 L.Ed.2d 985 (2000), [a]ttorneys[’]
       failure to file an appeal in spite of being
                        USA V. ANDERSON                        5


       instructed to do so is per se ineffective
       assistance.[]

    The district court ordered the government to respond and
directed Anderson’s trial counsel to address Anderson’s
allegations by way of a declaration. The government filed a
declaration from Anderson’s trial counsel that denied
Anderson asked him to file an appeal. Trial counsel further
stated that he consulted his co-counsel, who also did not
recall Anderson’s request to appeal, and reviewed his notes,
which did not reference any such request.
    The district court denied Anderson’s motion without a
hearing. It concluded that Anderson did not allege that he
directed counsel to appeal after sentencing, because his
motion said that he merely “discussed with trial counsel his
desire to appeal” after sentencing. The district court also
found that trial counsel’s affidavit “thoroughly contradicted”
any claim that Anderson directed his counsel to appeal. And
because “both parties . . . already submitted . . . their
respective versions of the events in question,” the district
court posited that “bringing them back into court to give
testimony that will almost certainly parrot their briefing
seem[ed] to be an unwarranted waste of judicial resources.”
The court also noted that it would be an “exercise in futility”
to grant a hearing because “Anderson knowingly and
voluntarily waived his appeal rights,” so “it appears . . . that
the ultimate dismissal of this case is a foregone conclusion.”
The district court thus held that it could “conclusively
determine Anderson’s credibility” without holding an
evidentiary hearing. Anderson appealed.
 6                      USA V. ANDERSON


                    Standard of Review
    We review de novo the district court’s denial of a § 2255
motion. United States v. Reves, 774 F.3d 562, 564 (9th Cir.
2014). We review for abuse of discretion the denial of an
evidentiary hearing. United States v. Chacon-Palomares,
208 F.3d 1157, 1158–59 (9th Cir. 2000).
                           Analysis
    When considering a § 2255 motion, the district court
must grant an evidentiary hearing “[u]nless the motion and
the files and records of the case conclusively show that the
prisoner is entitled to no relief.” 28 U.S.C. § 2255(b). A
hearing is thus required if “the movant has made specific
factual allegations that, if true, state a claim on which relief
could be granted.” United States v. Withers, 638 F.3d 1055,
1062 (9th Cir. 2011) (citation modified). But “[a]n oral
hearing is not necessary in all cases.” United States v.
Rodriguez-Vega, 797 F.3d 781, 791 (9th Cir. 2015). District
courts may “expand the record” with “discovery and
documentary evidence,” which satisfies the hearing
requirement if the motion can “be conclusively decided on
the basis of documentary testimony and evidence in the
record.” Watts v. United States, 841 F.2d 275, 277 (9th Cir.
1988) (per curiam); see also Shah v. United States, 878 F.2d
1156, 1159 (9th Cir. 1989).
    Here, Anderson’s allegations stated a claim for
ineffective assistance of counsel, and the expanded record
did not conclusively establish that those allegations were
false. A hearing was thus required.
                        USA V. ANDERSON                       7


I. Anderson’s allegations, if true, state a claim for
   ineffective assistance of counsel.
    To state a claim for ineffective assistance of counsel, a
movant must allege that his counsel’s representation was
(1) deficient and (2) prejudicial. Roe v. Flores-Ortega, 528
U.S. 470, 476–77 (2000). Both elements are met when a
lawyer fails to file a notice of appeal after his client
instructed him to do so. Garza v. Idaho, 586 U.S. 232, 241–
42 (2019). This is true even when the defendant waived his
right to appeal, see id. at 242–43, because the prejudice “is
that the defendant lost his chance to file the appeal, not that
he lost a favorable result that he would have obtained by
appeal.” United States v. Sandoval-Lopez, 409 F.3d 1193,
1197 (9th Cir. 2005).
    The district court concluded that Anderson alleged that
he merely “discussed” an appeal after sentencing but did not
allege that he instructed his counsel to appeal. Not so. While
Anderson alleged he “discussed” his “desire to appeal,” he
also alleged that his trial counsel “fail[ed] to file an
appeal . . . [a]fter the court[’]s imposition of sentence, and
after [Anderson] had directed trial counsel to file an appeal.”
We must construe Anderson’s pro se motion liberally and
give him “the benefit of any doubt.” Brown v. Roe, 279 F.3d
742, 746 (9th Cir. 2002) (citation modified). And we have
held that a pro se petitioner’s allegation that “he asked his
lawyer to file an appeal and his lawyer refused” is “specific
enough” to state a claim for ineffective assistance. Sandoval-
Lopez, 409 F.3d at 1198. So too here.
 8                      USA V. ANDERSON


II. The district court abused its discretion by holding
    that Anderson’s credibility could be “conclusively
    decided” without a hearing.
   Because Anderson’s motion stated a claim for relief, he
was entitled to a hearing unless the record “conclusively
show[ed]” that his claim failed. Withers, 638 F.3d at 1062;
Watts, 841 F.2d at 277; Shah, 878 F.2d at 1159.
    The district court was faced with two contradictory
sworn statements: (1) Anderson’s sworn statement that he
directed his trial counsel to appeal, and (2) trial counsel’s
sworn statement that Anderson’s statement “was not true”
and that counsel “had no recollection of such a request.”
Because credibility “can rarely be conclusive” based only on
declarations, the district court needed something more to
discern the truthfulness of one statement over the other.
United States v. Werle, 35 F.4th 1195, 1201 n.3 (9th Cir.
2022) (citation modified). For example, “seeing a witness
testify live assists the finder of fact in evaluating the
witness’s credibility.” United States v. Mejia, 69 F.3d 309,
315 (9th Cir. 1995). Indeed, “[l]ive testimony enables the
finder of fact to see the witness’s physical reactions to
questions, to assess the witness’s demeanor, and to hear the
tone of the witness’s voice—matters that cannot be gleaned
from a written [statement].” Id.
    The district court acknowledged that courts are “required
to hold an evidentiary hearing” when, as here, the parties file
conflicting statements “as to whether a petitioner did or did
not ask his trial counsel to file an appeal.” Yet rather than
hold a hearing, the district court concluded that a hearing
would be an “exercise in futility” and a “waste of judicial
resources.” This was an abuse of discretion. First, the futility
of a defendant’s underlying appeal is irrelevant to an
                       USA V. ANDERSON                       9


ineffective assistance of counsel claim. Supreme Court and
circuit precedent make clear that, when an attorney “fail[s]
to file a notice of appeal despite the defendant’s express
instructions, prejudice is presumed ‘with no further showing
from the defendant of the merits of his underlying claims.’”
See Garza, 586 U.S. at 247 (quoting Flores-Ortega, 528
U.S. at 484). In other words, a defendant need only show that
counsel deprived him “of an appeal that he otherwise would
have taken,” not that his appeal would succeed. Flores-
Ortega, 528 U.S. at 484. Second, judicial efficiency is not a
valid basis to deny an evidentiary hearing on a § 2255
motion. Deciding the motion based on the record will almost
always be more efficient than holding a hearing. But the
movant is entitled to a hearing unless the documentary
evidence “conclusively show[s]” that he is not entitled to
relief. Watts, 841 F.2d at 278; 28 U.S.C. § 2255(b).
    The government argues that this is a rare case in which
credibility can be “conclusively decided” on the record. We
disagree. The record can conclusively establish a habeas
petitioner’s credibility when his allegations are “so far
outside the bounds of reason” that they are “impossible to
believe.” See Shah, 878 F.2d at 1161–62; Watts, 841 F.2d at
278. That is not the case here. In Watts, for example, the
petitioner alleged that he reached a “secret” agreement with
the prosecution that, if he pled guilty, he would be sentenced
to no more than twenty years and his wife would be
sentenced to no more than two years. 841 F.2d at 276–77.
The petitioner pled guilty, but he was sentenced to life, and
his wife was sentenced to ten years. Id. at 277. After
sentencing, he wrote to the court multiple times and never
mentioned the alleged secret agreement. Id. at 278. Fourteen
months after sentencing, he filed a § 2255 motion raising the
alleged secret agreement for the first time. Id. at 277. On a
 10                    USA V. ANDERSON


record that included the plea hearing, several affidavits,
interrogatories of the petitioner and his wife, and the
petitioner’s letters to the court, the court “conclusively
decided” the petitioner’s credibility and denied the motion
without a hearing. Id. at 276–78.
    In contrast here, it is not “impossible to believe” that
Anderson told his counsel to appeal. See id. at 278.
Anderson’s § 2255 motion was his first filing in the district
court after his appeal deadline passed. That his plea
agreement included an appellate-waiver provision does not
deem his allegations incredible. Anderson could have
appealed, for instance, on the basis that the waiver was not
knowing or voluntary or that some exception applies. Or
Anderson may have simply misunderstood the scope of the
waiver. Either way, an appeal waiver does not undermine a
defendant’s claim that he asked his counsel to file an appeal.
Nor is such a claim unusual. See, e.g., Garza, 586 U.S. at
242–44 (holding that the presumption of prejudice applies
when a defendant shows that “counsel’s constitutionally
deficient performance deprived him of an appeal,” even
when he signed an appeal waiver (citation modified));
Sandoval-Lopez, 409 F.3d at 1195, 1198 (requiring an
evidentiary hearing to determine whether the petitioner
“asked his lawyer to file an appeal and his lawyer refused,”
even though the petitioner signed “as solid a waiver of the
right to appeal as can be imagined”).
     At bottom, when faced with two conflicting
statements—one from Anderson claiming he told his trial
counsel to appeal, and one from trial counsel claiming
otherwise—the district court could not conclusively credit
trial counsel’s version without the benefit of an evidentiary
hearing. See Sandoval-Lopez, 409 F.3d at 1198 (explaining
that a hearing was necessary “to determine whether [the
                      USA V. ANDERSON                     11


petitioner] really did tell his lawyer to appeal”); Chacon-
Palomares, 208 F.3d at 1159–60 (holding that an evidentiary
hearing was required to assess credibility when the expanded
record included “conflicting affidavits”).
                        Conclusion
    Anderson stated a claim for ineffective assistance of
counsel by alleging that his lawyer failed to file an appeal
after Anderson directed him to do so. The lawyer’s
conflicting declaration did not conclusively show that
Anderson’s allegations were false. We thus remand to the
district court for an evidentiary hearing.
   VACATED AND REMANDED.

court after his appeal deadline passed. That his plea
agreement included an appellate-waiver provision does not
deem his allegations incredible. Anderson could have
appealed, for instance, on the basis that the waiver was not
knowing or voluntary or that some exception applies. Or
Anderson may have simply misunderstood the scope of the
waiver. Either way, an appeal waiver does not undermine a
defendant’s claim that he asked his counsel to file an appeal.
Nor is such a claim unusual. See, e.g., Garza, 586 U.S. at
242–44 (holding that the presumption of prejudice applies
when a defendant shows that “counsel’s constitutionally
deficient performance deprived him of an appeal,” even
when he signed an appeal waiver (citation modified));
Sandoval-Lopez,
409 F.3d at 1195, 1198
 (requiring an
evidentiary hearing to determine whether the petitioner
“asked his lawyer to file an appeal and his lawyer refused,”
even though the petitioner signed “as solid a waiver of the
right to appeal as can be imagined”).
     At bottom, when faced with two conflicting
statements—one from Anderson claiming he told his trial
counsel to appeal, and one from trial counsel claiming
otherwise—the district court could not conclusively credit
trial counsel’s version without the benefit of an evidentiary
hearing. See Sandoval-Lopez,
409 F.3d at 1198
 (explaining
that a hearing was necessary “to determine whether [the
                      USA V. ANDERSON                     11


petitioner] really did tell his lawyer to appeal”); Chacon-
Palomares, 208 F.3d at 1159–60 (holding that an evidentiary
hearing was required to assess credibility when the expanded
record included “conflicting affidavits”).
                        Conclusion
    Anderson stated a claim for ineffective assistance of
counsel by alleging that his lawyer failed to file an appeal
after Anderson directed him to do so. The lawyer’s
conflicting declaration did not conclusively show that
Anderson’s allegations were false. We thus remand to the
district court for an evidentiary hearing.
   VACATED AND REMANDED.
